strands.title: Predict and connect
strands.description: Use relevant knowledge and textual clues to form a prediction, then revise it when new evidence appears.

strands.title: Question and investigate
strands.description: Ask useful questions, locate details, infer carefully, and choose evidence that supports a conclusion.

strands.title: Clarify and explore words
strands.description: Notice confusion, use context and word parts, and reread with a clear purpose.

strands.title: Summarize and synthesize
strands.description: Separate central ideas from minor details, summarize accurately, and connect information across a text.

lessons.title: Read the sky before the hike

model.text: At 8:00, clouds gathered over the ridge. The hikers packed their rain covers before starting uphill.
model.think: The clouds are a clue, and hikers usually prepare when weather may change. I predict rain is possible, but I will keep the prediction open until I read more.

guided.text: Mina set a paper pinwheel beside the garden. The air was still, but the weather report showed a wide band of wind moving toward the town.
guided.question: What is the strongest prediction about the pinwheel?
options: It may begin to turn when the wind arrives.
It will become a flower by the afternoon.
It has already broken because the air is still.
feedback: Use the approaching wind as a clue. A prediction should connect the report to what may happen next.
The passage gives no clue that a pinwheel can turn into a flower.
The still air describes now; it does not show that the pinwheel is broken.
guided.explanation: The wind is moving toward town, so it may reach the pinwheel later. The prediction uses a clue without claiming certainty.
guided.revise: Revise your prediction so it names both the clue and what may happen.

independent.text: The museum opened its rooftop telescope after sunset. A thin layer of clouds covered the eastern sky, while the west remained clear. The guide turned the telescope toward the west and asked visitors to wait for the Moon to rise.
independent.question: What will visitors most likely do while they wait?
options: Look toward the clearer western sky first.
Close the museum because every part of the sky is cloudy.
Move the Moon closer to the roof.
independent.explanation: The west is clear and the guide points the telescope that way. That evidence supports looking west first.
independent.transfer: Name a clue that could make you revise this prediction.

lessons.title: A shelf for the next season

model.text: A school saves seeds from its strongest plants. The label says the seeds will be planted after the last frost.
model.think: I connect the label to what I know about planting seasons. I predict the seeds will be used later, after cold weather eases.

guided.text: The class placed bean seeds in labeled envelopes. Their chart shows that the soil is still frozen, and the next check is scheduled for Friday.
guided.question: What is a reasonable next step for the class?
options: Check the soil again on Friday before planting.
Plant all the seeds in frozen soil today.
Throw away the chart because it mentions Friday.
feedback: The scheduled check and frozen soil suggest waiting to see whether conditions change.
Frozen soil is evidence that planting now may not work well.
The chart gives useful timing information; the text does not suggest discarding it.
guided.explanation: The class has a planned check and the soil is frozen now, so checking again before planting fits the evidence.
guided.revise: Complete this sentence: Because the soil is ___, the class may ___.

independent.text: A neighborhood group collected rainwater in covered barrels. The weather notice predicts a dry week, and the garden beds were watered yesterday. The group put a note on the barrels to measure how much water remains on Monday.
independent.question: Why will the group probably measure the water on Monday?
options: To check the supply after the dry days.
To prove that rain never falls in the neighborhood.
To make the barrels heavier before watering.
independent.explanation: The dry forecast makes the remaining supply important, and Monday is the planned check.
independent.transfer: What new weather clue could change the group's plan?

model.text: Workers test each bridge light before dusk. A report says one light stayed dark during the morning test.
model.think: The test result is a clue about a possible problem. I predict workers will inspect that light, rather than assume every light failed.

guided.text: At noon, a park worker placed a small barrier near the bridge entrance. A ladder and a box of replacement bulbs stood beside the dark lamp.
guided.question: What is the worker most likely preparing to do?
options: Repair or replace the dark lamp.
Paint the river under the bridge.
Move the bridge to another park.
feedback: The barrier, ladder, and bulbs are clues connected to lamp repair.
Nothing in the passage connects the equipment to painting the river.
The passage gives no evidence that the bridge will be moved.
guided.explanation: The ladder and replacement bulbs support the prediction that the worker will repair the lamp.
guided.revise: Which two clues support your revised prediction?

independent.text: A librarian wheeled a cart of picture books into the courtyard. Dark clouds were forming, so she set a waterproof cover on top of the books and checked the sky again before opening the cart.
independent.question: What is the librarian likely to do before readers choose books?
options: Make sure the books are protected from possible rain.
Leave the cart outside during a storm without checking it.
Replace the books with gardening tools.
independent.explanation: The cover and sky check show the librarian is preparing for possible rain.
independent.transfer: Explain how the librarian might change plans if the sky clears.

model.text: A delivery robot paused at a curb. Its route map showed a closed street ahead and a marked crosswalk to the north.
model.think: I combine two clues: the street is closed, and a crosswalk is mapped nearby. I predict a route change is likely, but the text must show the robot's choice.

guided.text: During the trial, a rover's sensor detected loose gravel on the planned path. The map showed a paved service lane running around the test area.
guided.question: Which action is best supported by the clues?
options: The rover may use the paved lane around the gravel.
The rover will dig through the gravel to reach the Moon.
The rover's sensor will stop detecting every surface.
feedback: The paved lane is a safer mapped alternative to the loose gravel.
The text describes a local test route, not a lunar mission or digging tool.
One detection does not prove that the sensor will stop working.
guided.explanation: The rover detected a hazard and has a paved alternative. That makes a route change plausible.
guided.revise: Write a prediction that includes the hazard and the alternative route.

independent.text: A coastal research team planned to collect shoreline samples at noon. The tide table showed unusually high water at that time, and a nearby platform remained above the marked tide line. The team moved its equipment toward the platform.
independent.question: What is the team most likely planning to do next?
options: Collect samples from a safer elevated location.
Ignore the tide table and leave the equipment below the water line.
Change the tide by moving its equipment.
independent.explanation: The high tide and elevated platform explain the team's move toward a safer sampling location.
independent.transfer: State what additional clue would help confirm your prediction.

model.text: An archivist found a box marked 'photographs—handle with care.' The box was stored on a high shelf above a work table.
model.think: The label signals that the contents may be fragile. I predict the archivist will move the box carefully to the table, using the label as evidence.

guided.text: A town archive discovered a set of letters with dates from the same winter. Several envelopes were sealed, and a note asked researchers to compare the addresses before opening them.
guided.question: What will researchers most likely do first?
options: Compare the addresses as the note requests.
Open every envelope before recording any information.
Discard the letters because they are old.
feedback: The note gives a clear first action and the addresses may show a relationship.
Opening them first ignores the stated comparison step.
The archive is preserving the letters for research, not discarding them.
guided.explanation: The instruction to compare addresses is the strongest clue about the researchers' next action.
guided.revise: Explain why following the note could help researchers.

independent.text: A geologist labeled two rock samples with the same site number but different depths. The field notebook described a clay layer between those depths. The geologist placed the samples side by side and opened the notebook to the layer diagram.
independent.question: What is the geologist most likely trying to determine?
options: How the rock samples relate to their different positions in the ground.
Whether the labels should be removed before any comparison.
How to turn the rock samples into a notebook.
independent.explanation: Different depths and the layer diagram help compare where the samples came from.
independent.transfer: What observation might lead the geologist to revise an initial prediction?

model.text: A radio club tuned an antenna toward a ridge. The schedule listed a strong signal test after sunset, when electrical noise usually decreases.
model.think: I connect the time of day with the expected signal conditions. I predict the test may be clearer after sunset, but I should check the result rather than treat the schedule as proof.

guided.text: A student team planned to compare bird calls near a busy road and in a quiet marsh. At the road, traffic noise covered several recordings. The marsh was calm that morning.
guided.question: Which comparison result is most plausible?
options: The marsh recordings may make some bird calls easier to hear.
Traffic noise will make the birds stop existing near the road.
The marsh recordings will contain no sound at all.
feedback: A quieter setting can make calls easier to distinguish in recordings.
The text says noise covered recordings; it does not say birds disappeared.
A quiet marsh can still contain bird calls and other sounds.
guided.explanation: The recordings at the road were masked by traffic, while the marsh was calm. That supports a clearer recording there.
guided.revise: Use 'may' or 'might' to show that this is a prediction, not a fact.

independent.text: Engineers tested a sensor beside a reflective wall. The sensor reported a second object whenever sunlight struck the wall at a low angle. The team scheduled another test with a shade panel placed over the wall.
independent.question: What is the purpose of the next test likely to be?
options: Check whether blocking the glare changes the sensor readings.
Prove that the sensor can never detect an object.
Move sunlight to a different season.
independent.explanation: The shade panel changes the glare condition that coincided with the extra reading.
independent.transfer: Name a result that would make the engineers revise this prediction.

model.text: A garden pump hummed for a few seconds and then stopped. A student wrote, 'The pump is broken.'
model.think: Before accepting that claim, I ask a question that can be investigated: Was the water tank empty, or did the pump lose power? A useful question points to evidence.

guided.text: The school fountain stopped flowing. The switch was on, but the water level in its storage tank had dropped below the marked line.
guided.question: Which question would best help investigate why the fountain stopped?
options: Is the tank's water level too low for the fountain to run?
What color is the fountain's stone?
Who first named the school?
feedback: This question connects the low water level to the fountain's operation.
The stone color does not help explain why water stopped flowing.
The school's name does not provide evidence about the fountain.
guided.explanation: The tank level is a relevant clue, so a question about whether it is too low can be tested.
guided.revise: Write one more question that could be answered by observing the fountain.

independent.text: A class planted three trays of seedlings. One tray leaned toward the window, while the other two stood upright under a lamp. The window tray had received less time under the lamp because it was moved during cleaning.
independent.question: Which question best investigates why the first tray leaned?
options: Did the tray receive less light than the others?
How many desks are in the classroom?
What is the window made of?
independent.explanation: The different light exposure is a relevant condition to investigate.
independent.transfer: Write a question that could test whether the seedlings lean toward light.

model.text: A trail map shows a blue dotted line and a small water symbol. The legend explains that dotted lines mark footpaths.
model.think: A reader can ask what a symbol means, then use the legend to answer. The question guides attention to a specific source of information.

guided.text: A map of the town park has a star beside one path. The legend says stars show places where visitors can refill water bottles.
guided.question: Which question can the legend answer directly?
options: What does the star mark on the map?
Who drew the map ten years ago?
How many visitors will come next summer?
feedback: The legend directly defines the star symbol.
The text does not name the mapmaker or give a date.
A map symbol cannot predict next summer's visitor count.
guided.explanation: The legend states that a star marks a bottle refill point.
guided.revise: Make a new question about a different symbol and identify where you would look.

independent.text: A diagram of a butterfly garden uses arrows to show the path of sunlight during the day. The arrows begin on the eastern side in the morning and move toward the western side by late afternoon.
independent.question: Which question can the diagram help answer?
options: From which direction does sunlight reach the garden first?
How many butterflies will hatch next year?
Who designed the first garden in the country?
independent.explanation: The arrows show the direction of sunlight at different times.
independent.transfer: Create a question about the diagram that would require an inference, not just a label.

lessons.title: A careful question about a vessel

model.text: A museum label says a clay bowl was found near a river. The bowl has a small hole near its rim.
model.think: I separate what is stated from what I wonder. The river location is a fact; the hole's purpose is not. I ask a question before making an inference.

guided.text: Archaeologists found a clay cup beside a cooking area. Its surface had dark patches, and nearby stones showed signs of heat.
guided.question: Which question is most closely connected to the evidence?
options: Could the dark patches be related to how the cup was used near heat?
What song did the archaeologists hear at lunch?
How tall is the nearest modern building?
feedback: This question connects the surface and nearby heat evidence.
The passage gives no evidence about music at lunch.
A modern building's height does not explain the ancient cup.
guided.explanation: A focused question links the dark patches to the heat-marked cooking area without claiming certainty.
guided.revise: Rewrite the question so it invites evidence rather than assumes an answer.

independent.text: A stone path ended beside a shallow stream. On the other bank, researchers found matching stone pieces. The pieces had similar shapes, but the passage did not describe how they arrived there.
independent.question: What is the most useful question to investigate next?
options: Could people have used the path to cross the stream?
What is the stream's favorite season?
Why did the stones decide to move?
independent.explanation: The path and matching stones on both banks are relevant clues about crossing.
independent.transfer: Name one additional piece of evidence that could help answer your question.

model.text: A team counts bats at the cave entrance during one evening. A single count tells how many passed at that time, not why the number changed.
model.think: I ask a question that separates possible explanations: Did temperature or time of year affect the count? Then I identify what data would help answer it.

guided.text: At a pond, researchers found fewer frog calls after a cold front. The water temperature had also dropped, and the team had not recorded rainfall that week.
guided.question: Which follow-up question would help compare possible causes?
options: How did water temperature and rainfall change across several evenings?
What color are the researchers' boots?
Can frogs read the weather forecast?
feedback: Repeated temperature and rainfall records can help compare the conditions.
Boot color is not related to the observed change in calls.
The passage provides no basis for that claim.
guided.explanation: Recording both conditions over time gives relevant evidence to examine possible relationships.
guided.revise: Add a time period to make the investigation question more precise.

independent.text: A city measured bicycle use on two streets. Street A had a protected bike lane and 42 riders on Tuesday. Street B had no protected lane and 29 riders on the same day. Both streets had different amounts of car traffic.
independent.question: Which question would help interpret the difference fairly?
options: How did rider counts and car traffic compare across more days?
Which street has the brighter sign?
Can one Tuesday prove why riders chose each street?
independent.explanation: More days and traffic data can help test whether the Tuesday difference is consistent and what conditions may relate to it.
independent.transfer: Name a comparison that would make the evidence stronger.

model.text: A web post says a new plant grows twice as fast in blue light. It shows one plant but gives no method or comparison.
model.think: I ask what comparison and measurement support the claim. A picture can show a plant, but it does not establish a growth rate by itself.

guided.text: Two reports describe a local bridge project. One gives a date and a measured water-flow change. The other says only that the project was 'a huge success.'
guided.question: Which question best evaluates the reports?
options: What measurements and time period support each report's claim?
Which report uses the most exciting adjectives?
What color is the bridge at sunset?
feedback: A claim can be checked against its measurements and time period.
Exciting language is not evidence of the project's effect.
The bridge's color does not test the reports' claims.
guided.explanation: Checking measures and time frames helps readers compare the quality of the evidence.
guided.revise: Explain why a measurement is more useful than an adjective for evaluating the claim.

independent.text: A school newsletter reports that a new seating plan improved group discussion. It includes student comments but no observation notes from before the change. The principal says the plan will be reviewed after another month.
independent.question: What question would most improve the evidence for the newsletter's claim?
options: How did discussion observations compare before and after the change?
Which student wrote the longest comment?
Why are chairs shaped differently?
independent.explanation: A before-and-after comparison of observations could help evaluate whether discussion changed.
independent.transfer: What limitation would remain even after collecting those observations?

model.text: After heavy rain, a river left silt on a field. A fence near the bank stood tilted, but the report did not say when it moved.
model.think: I can infer that water reached the field, because silt was left there. I cannot conclude the rain tilted the fence without timing evidence.

guided.text: A photograph taken Monday showed dry pavement near the creek. By Tuesday, leaves and a thin mud line marked the path. Rain had fallen overnight.
guided.question: Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Water likely reached part of the path after the rain.
The creek permanently changed its course.
Every leaf in the area came from one tree.
feedback: The mud line, leaves, and overnight rain support temporary water reaching the path.
One observation does not prove a permanent change in the creek's course.
The passage does not identify where every leaf came from.
guided.explanation: The evidence supports a limited inference about water reaching the path, not a permanent or universal claim.
guided.revise: Narrow your conclusion so it says only what the clues support.

independent.text: In a city survey, most shaded bus stops had lower surface temperatures than nearby unshaded stops on the same afternoon. The report noted that the stops were measured at slightly different times.
independent.question: Which inference is most careful?
options: Shade may be related to lower surface temperatures, though timing is a limitation.
Shade always lowers every city's temperature by the same amount.
The survey proves that stop location never matters.
independent.explanation: The observed pattern supports a possible relationship, but different measurement times limit certainty.
independent.transfer: Identify another variable the survey could measure.

lessons.title: Use context to clarify a word

model.text: The guide said the trail became narrow near the ravine, so the hikers walked single file.
model.think: The phrase 'walked single file' gives a clue: the trail is not wide. I use the surrounding action to clarify narrow.

guided.text: The seedling was fragile. Its stem bent when the class moved the pot, so they carried it with both hands.
guided.question: What does fragile most nearly mean here?
options: Easily damaged
Able to grow without water
Very tall
feedback: The bending stem and careful carrying show that the seedling can be damaged easily.
The text says nothing about growing without water.
Height does not explain why the class handled it carefully.
guided.explanation: The stem bends during movement, so fragile means easily damaged in this sentence.
guided.revise: Use the clue 'carried it with both hands' to write a meaning for fragile.

independent.text: When the old gate began to wobble, the caretaker braced it with a wooden support. She checked the hinges again before allowing students through.
independent.question: What does braced most nearly mean in this passage?
options: Supported so it would stay steady
Painted a bright color
Removed from the path
independent.explanation: The wooden support and hinge check show that braced means supported to make stable.
independent.transfer: Write a different sentence that uses braced with a clear context clue.

model.text: The class planted a row of beans. At the end of the row, a sign marked the place where the next seeds would go.
model.think: A word can have more than one meaning. I read the whole sentence and choose the meaning that fits the planting context.

guided.text: The team will pitch its tent beside the lake. They checked the ground first so the tent would stay level.
guided.question: What does pitch mean in this sentence?
options: Set up or place
Throw a ball
The highness of a musical sound
feedback: The tent and level ground show that pitch means set up here.
No ball is mentioned; the object is a tent.
The passage is about camping, not music.
guided.explanation: The camping context determines which meaning of pitch fits.
guided.revise: Write a clue from the passage that helps rule out the ball meaning.

independent.text: The class studied a bat resting inside a dark cave. Later, they used a wooden bat during a game on the field.
independent.question: Which statement best explains the two uses of bat?
options: The same spelling has two meanings that the surrounding sentences clarify.
Both sentences describe the same animal.
The word has no meaning in either sentence.
independent.explanation: Cave and resting point to the animal; wooden and game point to sports equipment.
independent.transfer: Write one context clue for each meaning of bat.

lessons.title: A word part gives a clue

model.text: A class reread a page after the teacher asked them to review it. The prefix re- often means again.
model.think: I combine the word part with the context: reread means read again. The sentence confirms the word-part clue.

guided.text: The students previewed the diagram before reading the article. They looked at its labels first to prepare for the information.
guided.question: What does previewed most nearly mean here?
options: Viewed beforehand
Viewed through a window
Viewed for the last time
feedback: The students looked at the diagram before reading, which matches pre- meaning before.
The passage does not describe looking through glass.
The action happens before reading, not necessarily for the last time.
guided.explanation: The prefix pre- means before, and the sequence confirms that meaning.
guided.revise: Use pre- and view to explain previewed in your own words.

independent.text: A reporter rewrote one sentence after checking the date. The corrected version made the timeline clearer for readers.
independent.question: What does rewrote most nearly mean?
options: Wrote again in a changed form
Wrote before the event happened
Wrote while looking through glass
independent.explanation: The reporter changed a sentence after checking it; re- means again.
independent.transfer: Find another familiar word beginning with re- and use context to explain it.

model.text: The class measured the height of several plants. A measurement is the result of measuring.
model.think: The ending -ment can turn an action word into a noun naming a result or thing. I check that idea against the sentence.

guided.text: The explorer's movement through the narrow tunnel was slow. She checked each foothold before taking another step.
guided.question: What does movement name in the sentence?
options: The act or process of moving
A tool used to measure a tunnel
A place where explorers sleep
feedback: The slow steps describe the process of moving.
Nothing in the text describes a measuring tool.
The passage describes travel through a tunnel, not a sleeping place.
guided.explanation: The ending -ment forms a noun naming the process of moving.
guided.revise: Complete: Movement is the process of ___.

independent.text: The scientist recorded an adjustment to the microscope. She turned one small dial until the image came into focus.
independent.question: What does adjustment refer to here?
options: A change made to improve the setting
A person who studies stars
A report about an animal
independent.explanation: Turning the dial is a change to the microscope's setting.
independent.transfer: Circle the word part in adjustment and explain what kind of word the ending helps create.

lessons.title: Use a root to explore meaning

model.text: A portable device can be carried from place to place. The root port relates to carrying.
model.think: The root gives a useful clue, but I still check how the whole word works in its sentence.

guided.text: The report described an import of rice arriving at the harbor. The rice had been grown in another country and brought into the region.
guided.question: What does import most nearly mean here?
options: Bring goods into a place
Carry goods away from a place
Measure the size of a harbor
feedback: The rice is brought into the region; im- can mean in, and the root relates to carrying.
The passage describes rice coming into the region, not leaving it.
The word is about goods moving, not measuring the harbor.
guided.explanation: The direction of movement and the word parts support the meaning bring goods in.
guided.revise: Explain how the sentence's direction clue helps confirm the root clue.

independent.text: A transport system moves people between neighborhoods. Its schedule lists buses that carry riders toward the city center and back again.
independent.question: What idea is shared by transport and portable?
options: Both relate to carrying or moving something from place to place.
Both describe a fixed point that cannot move.
Both mean to record information in a chart.
independent.explanation: The shared root port connects both words to carrying or movement.
independent.transfer: Use transport in a new sentence that makes its meaning clear.

model.text: A paragraph says a metal cooled quickly, but the reason is unclear. I reread the sentence before and after it to find the material comparison.
model.think: Rereading works best with a question. I am looking for the detail that explains why cooling happened quickly, not starting over without a purpose.

guided.text: The article says the wetland filtered water before it reached the lake. The next sentence explains that soil and plant roots trapped some particles.
guided.question: What should a reader reread to clarify how filtering happens?
options: The sentence about soil and roots trapping particles
The title only
A paragraph about an unrelated bird count
feedback: That sentence explains the process named by filtering.
The title may name the topic but does not explain the process.
A bird count does not clarify how soil and roots filter water.
guided.explanation: The process detail directly explains how the wetland filters water.
guided.revise: State your rereading question before naming the sentence you would revisit.

independent.text: A history text says the new rail line changed the market. A later paragraph explains that farmers could send produce to distant towns before it spoiled.
independent.question: Which section should you reread to clarify how the rail line changed the market?
options: The paragraph connecting transport time with produce sales
A caption about the station's color
A section listing unrelated weather records
independent.explanation: The later paragraph gives the cause connecting rail travel with market changes.
independent.transfer: Write a focused rereading question about the link between travel time and sales.

lessons.title: Use contrast to clarify a term

model.text: Unlike the brittle sample, the flexible strip bent without cracking. The contrast helps explain both terms.
model.think: Signal words such as unlike point to a contrast. I use the known action to clarify the unfamiliar description.

guided.text: The first trial was precise: each container received exactly 20 milliliters. The second was less consistent because the measuring marks were difficult to see.
guided.question: What does precise most nearly mean in this passage?
options: Accurate and exact
Very colorful
Difficult to carry
feedback: The exact 20 milliliters shows that precise means accurate or exact.
Color is not part of the measurement description.
The passage discusses accuracy, not carrying.
guided.explanation: The exact amount is a context clue for precise.
guided.revise: Use the contrast with the second trial to explain precise.

independent.text: The first route was direct, with no turns between the station and the library. The alternate route was indirect, winding through three side streets.
independent.question: What does direct mean in the passage?
options: Following a straight or uncomplicated path
Moving secretly
Taking a longer winding path
independent.explanation: The contrast with the winding alternate route shows that direct means uncomplicated or straight.
independent.transfer: Write a sentence that uses indirect and includes a context clue.

model.text: A paragraph names sea grass, young fish, and small crabs. It explains that the plants give these animals places to hide.
model.think: The central idea connects the details: sea grass provides shelter for small animals. The list of animals supports the idea but is not the whole message.

guided.text: A school added native plants beside its playground. The plants provide shade, attract butterflies, and help hold soil in place when it rains.
guided.question: Which sentence best states the central idea?
options: Native plants provide several benefits beside the playground.
Butterflies have wings.
It rained one afternoon.
feedback: This sentence brings together the shade, wildlife, and soil details.
That is a detail about butterflies, not the passage's main point.
Rain is one condition; it does not summarize the benefits.
guided.explanation: The details all support the broader idea that native plants help the playground in several ways.
guided.revise: Combine two supporting details under one central idea.

independent.text: A community repaired an old footpath. Volunteers cleared branches, rebuilt two steps, and added signs showing where the path meets the road. The work made the route safer and easier to follow.
independent.question: Which sentence best summarizes the central idea?
options: The community improved a footpath so people can use it more safely.
There were exactly two steps on the path.
Branches can fall onto a trail.
independent.explanation: The sentence captures the purpose that connects the repair details.
independent.transfer: Name one detail that supports the central idea.

model.text: A student puts soil in a pot, places a seed, covers it, and waters it. These steps describe how the seed is planted.
model.think: A summary keeps the steps in order but leaves out minor actions that do not change the process.

guided.text: First, workers sort clean cans by size. Next, a machine presses them into compact bundles. Finally, the bundles are sent to a recycling center.
guided.question: Which summary keeps the important sequence?
options: Workers sort cans, press them into bundles, and send them to be recycled.
Workers look at cans while standing near a machine.
The recycling center sorts workers into groups.
feedback: This summary preserves the three main steps in order.
It leaves out the process and focuses on an unimportant action.
It changes who is being sorted and does not match the passage.
guided.explanation: A sequence summary names the important actions in the order they occur.
guided.revise: Retell the three steps using first, next, and finally.

independent.text: To prepare a classroom map, students measure the room, mark the doors and windows, and draw desks in their locations. They add a key so a reader can understand each symbol.
independent.question: Which summary best preserves the process?
options: Students measure, map features and desks, then add a key for the symbols.
Students draw a key before knowing what the symbols mean.
The room has desks and windows.
independent.explanation: The summary keeps the major actions and their sequence.
independent.transfer: Which step would make the map difficult to read if it were skipped? Explain why.

model.text: A report says a turtle crossed a path to reach a pond. It also notes that the path was painted green last year.
model.think: The painting detail does not explain the turtle's movement. A concise summary keeps what matters to the main event.

guided.text: A team found a safe way to move a heavy table. They placed a cloth under each leg and slid the table slowly. The cloth was blue with yellow stars.
guided.question: Which summary keeps the essential information?
options: The team used cloth under the legs to slide the table safely.
The cloth had yellow stars.
The table was heavy and stood in a room.
feedback: This includes the problem and the important solution.
The pattern is a minor detail that does not explain the solution.
This names objects but omits the key action.
guided.explanation: A summary includes the problem-solving action, not decorative details.
guided.revise: Cross out one detail that does not help explain the solution.

independent.text: A class designed a shade screen using measured fabric and clips. They tested it over the reading bench and adjusted two clips when the screen sagged. The fabric had a striped pattern.
independent.question: Which summary is most useful?
options: Students tested a shade screen and adjusted clips so it would hang properly.
The fabric had stripes.
The bench was used for reading.
independent.explanation: The summary captures the design, test, and adjustment that are central to the passage.
independent.transfer: Identify a detail you would omit and explain why.

model.text: The path flooded after a storm because a drain was blocked with leaves. Workers cleared the drain, and the water receded.
model.think: A useful summary keeps the cause and the result. The leaves explain the flooding; clearing the drain explains why water went down.

guided.text: A classroom plant drooped after a hot weekend. The soil was dry, so the class watered it and moved it away from the sunny window.
guided.question: Which summary best connects the cause and response?
options: The plant drooped in dry heat, so students watered it and reduced its sun exposure.
The window was beside the plant.
The class watered a different plant during winter.
feedback: This links the condition to the actions students took.
The window is only a location detail.
The passage does not mention a different plant or winter.
guided.explanation: The dry soil and hot window are clues for the drooping, and the students respond to those conditions.
guided.revise: Use because or so to connect a cause with an effect.

independent.text: After several weeks without rain, the soil on a slope became loose. Heavy rain washed some soil into the road. Workers planted grasses whose roots can hold soil in place.
independent.question: Which summary best describes the cause and response?
options: Dry conditions loosened soil, rain carried it away, and workers planted grasses to stabilize the slope.
Workers planted grass because roads need paint.
Rain stopped because the grasses were already there.
independent.explanation: The summary preserves the sequence from dry soil to erosion to a response.
independent.transfer: What evidence would help determine whether the grass reduced erosion?

model.text: One source says trees cool streets with shade. Another says leaves release water vapor that can cool nearby air.
model.think: I connect the shared idea without pretending the sources say exactly the same thing: both describe ways trees can reduce heat.

guided.text: A park survey reports that visitors use shaded benches at midday. A second report measures lower surface temperatures beneath the park's trees than on nearby pavement.
guided.question: Which synthesis connects both sources accurately?
options: The reports suggest that tree shade is useful to visitors and is associated with cooler surfaces.
Both reports prove that every visitor prefers every tree.
The survey and temperature report describe unrelated places.
feedback: This combines visitor use with the measured temperature pattern and keeps the claim limited.
The reports do not support a universal claim about every visitor.
Both sources concern the park and its shade.
guided.explanation: The synthesis links both findings while keeping the conclusion within the evidence.
guided.revise: Add one word that signals the evidence suggests a relationship rather than proving cause.

independent.text: A science text explains that wetlands slow flowing water and trap some sediment. A local project report says restored marsh plants reduced the amount of soil reaching a nearby inlet during two storms.
independent.question: Which synthesis is best supported?
options: Wetland plants can slow water and may reduce sediment reaching an inlet, as shown in the two-storm report.
Wetlands stop every flood everywhere.
The local report measured fish color rather than soil.
independent.explanation: The conclusion connects the general process with the local observation and avoids overgeneralizing.
independent.transfer: What further evidence would help test whether the effect continues over time?

model.text: A student argues that the library should stay open later because many students ride buses home. The student also notes that the library has quiet study spaces.
model.think: A fair summary states the main claim and its strongest reason without adding my opinion or a reason the writer did not give.

guided.text: A neighborhood group supports adding a crosswalk near the market. Members say many families cross there, and cars often turn quickly at the corner.
guided.question: Which summary represents the group's position fairly?
options: The group wants a crosswalk because many families cross near a fast-turning corner.
The group dislikes every driver in the neighborhood.
The market should close because families shop there.
feedback: This states the position and the reasons given.
The passage does not make a claim about every driver.
The group supports a crosswalk; it does not ask for the market to close.
guided.explanation: A fair summary preserves the position and reasons without adding a judgment.
guided.revise: Check that your summary includes a claim and a reason from the passage.

independent.text: A student council proposal asks the school to open a supervised study room twice a week. The proposal says students who stay for activities need a place to work before late buses arrive. It does not ask the school to add more homework.
independent.question: Which summary best represents the proposal?
options: The council proposes a twice-weekly study room for students waiting for late buses.
The council wants teachers to assign more homework every day.
The council opposes all after-school activities.
independent.explanation: The summary gives the proposed action, schedule, and reason without adding unsupported ideas.
independent.transfer: What important detail should a reader preserve when summarizing this proposal?

lessons.title: Summarize a pattern and its limit

model.text: A table shows that three measured blocks had more bike trips on sunny days than on rainy days. It covers one month.
model.think: The central idea is a pattern in the measured month. I include the time limit so the summary does not sound universal.

guided.text: A class tracked paper use for four weeks. After students used both sides of each sheet, the weekly total fell in three of the four weeks. The school had a holiday during one week.
guided.question: Which summary is most accurate?
options: Paper use fell in most tracked weeks after the class changed its routine, with one holiday week as a difference.
Paper use always falls whenever students use both sides.
The class tracked paper use for four years.
feedback: This captures the pattern and notes the unusual week.
The limited data do not support an always claim.
The passage states four weeks, not four years.
guided.explanation: An accurate summary reports the observed pattern and preserves its limits.
guided.revise: Add the time period to make the statement more precise.

independent.text: A school compared library visits for six Mondays before and after a new lunchtime schedule. Visits increased on four Mondays after the change. Two Mondays had special events that changed the library's hours.
independent.question: Which summary best fits the data?
options: Visits were higher on four of six Mondays after the schedule change, though two days had different hours.
The new schedule caused every student to visit the library.
Visits fell on all six Mondays after the schedule change.
independent.explanation: This summary reports the actual pattern and notes a condition that limits comparison.
independent.transfer: What other information would you want before explaining why visits changed?
